subject: Communication
title: TED Talks: The New Oratory Standard
description: A micro-lesson that makes TED Talks: The New Oratory Standard usable.

hook.text: In 2006, TED started posting talks online for free. Public speaking would never be the same.

buildup.text: Suddenly, millions could watch world-class speakers. A new standard for presentation quality emerged.

discovery.text: The TED formula: one big idea, personal stories, minimal slides, and an 18-minute limit.

twist.text: TED democratized speaking but also created pressure. Now every conference expects 'TED-level' talks.

climax.text: The most-viewed TED talk has over 75 million views — more than most blockbuster movies' opening weekends.

punchline.text: TED proved that great ideas, well told, travel the world.

quiz.question: When did TED start posting talks online for free?

details.summary: TED Talks have redefined public speaking for the digital age. The 18-minute format, emphasis on one clear idea, and storytelling-driven structure have created a new template that influences presentations worldwide. TED proved that ideas, not credentials, are the ultimate currency on stage.
details.whyItMatters: TED democratized great speaking. It proved that anyone with a compelling idea and strong delivery can reach millions, regardless of institutional backing.
takeaways: The 18-minute format is based on attention and retention science
One talk, one idea is the core structural principle
TED proved online video can make speakers globally influential

faq.question: Why is the TED Talk format set at 18 minutes?
faq.answer: TED curator Chris Anderson chose 18 minutes because it is long enough to develop a serious idea but short enough to hold attention. It forces speakers to be concise and eliminates padding. The constraint itself improves the talk by requiring ruthless editing of content.

faq.question: What makes a TED Talk succeed versus fail?
faq.answer: Successful talks have one clear idea, a strong opening hook, personal stories that illustrate the concept, and a memorable closing. Failed talks try to cover too much, rely on credentials instead of narrative, or present information without emotional engagement or practical relevance.
